focus: Success can blur the original cause because growth rewards measurable WHATs while the founding WHY becomes assumed, nostalgic, or hard to articulate.
coreClaim: Organizations begin to lose inspiration when the visible products, prices, and metrics keep expanding after the original purpose has stopped guiding decisions.

centralConcept.name: fuzzy WHY
centralConcept.plainDefinition: A fuzzy WHY is a purpose that once felt clear but no longer directs choices with enough force. The organization may still be successful, but outsiders and insiders increasingly recognize outputs rather than belief.
centralConcept.whyItMatters: A reader who recognizes fuzziness can treat success as a risk signal, not only a validation signal. Growth creates distance from origin stories, founders, and early believers unless the cause is made explicit and operational.

keyClaims: Early success often depends on a founder or small group embodying a cause before it is formally written down.
As scale increases, leaders pay more attention to revenue, market share, efficiency, legal exposure, and competitor comparison.
WHAT-level success can hide WHY-level erosion because sales and size may continue after meaning weakens.
A product extension can contradict the founding belief even when it is well engineered or prestigious.
Public reputation changes when the audience can no longer connect a company's actions to the values it once represented.
Founder death, leadership transition, and rapid growth make fuzziness more likely because the living source of the cause becomes distant.
The warning sign is not failure but success without the same clarity that created the following.

namedExamples.label: Volkswagen Phaeton
namedExamples.summary: Volkswagen's name and heritage point toward a car for ordinary people, with the Beetle symbolizing accessibility, simplicity, and freedom. The high-priced Phaeton contradicted that meaning by asking buyers to see Volkswagen as a luxury prestige brand.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: A technically capable WHAT can fail when it violates the WHY people associate with the brand.

namedExamples.label: Wal-Mart after Sam Walton
namedExamples.summary: Wal-Mart grew from Sam Walton's people-centered value idea into a massive retail machine. After Walton's death, public attention increasingly attached to wages, lawsuits, community resistance, and ruthless low-cost execution rather than the original service-to-people spirit.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: Scale can preserve the operating model while losing the human cause that once made the model inspiring.

hardEdge: The easy lesson is to avoid luxury extensions or protect a founder's legacy sentimentally. The harder lesson is that successful metrics can conceal purpose decay; an organization can keep winning on WHAT while the belief that made people care becomes too fuzzy to guide hard choices.
voiceCues: uses decline stories from recognizable brands rather than start-up failure stories
makes success itself the source of danger
contrasts heritage symbols with later business decisions
keeps the warning practical by tying fuzziness to reputation, employees, and product permission
paraphraseNotes: The danger shifts from lacking success to surviving it. A young organization often has a vivid source of meaning because the founder or founding group personally carries the cause. People close to the origin do not need elaborate explanation; they can feel why the work matters. Growth changes that. More employees join who never lived the origin. More decisions are made through metrics, legal caution, margin targets, expansion pressure, and competitor comparison. The visible WHAT may keep growing while the inner cause weakens. Volkswagen's Phaeton makes the contradiction concrete. The brand's name and Beetle history evoke accessible cars for ordinary people, yet the Phaeton asked the public to accept Volkswagen as a luxury prestige badge. The engineering could be strong and still feel wrong because the product strained the inherited meaning. Wal-Mart supplies a cultural version. Sam Walton's low-price model carried a people-centered promise about helping customers, employees, and communities. After his death, public attention increasingly attached to the machinery of low cost: lawsuits, wages, expansion battles, and efficiency at human expense. Fuzzy WHY is therefore not the same as collapse. It is the period when the organization still has power, money, and reach, but the public can no longer hear the original cause clearly through its actions.
